title: Cap. X Arg. X: adversaries put Peter and Judas under the same sufficient grace — free-will use separates them; that contradicts 1 Cor. iv. 7 Quis te discernit?
pass_a_gloss: Concerning the consequence there can be no doubt, because from the adversaries’ sentence, sufficient grace unto believing and repenting having been administered both unto Judas and unto Peter, the good use of free will embracing this sufficient grace commonly offered unto both placed Peter in the number of believers and elect, and the bad use of free will thrusting back the same shut Judas out from the number of believers and elect. But this diametrically opposes that Pauline sentence 1 Cor. iv. 7, Who discerns thee? what hast thou which thou didst not receive? and if thou didst receive, why dost thou glory as if thou didst not receive?
pass_b_english: The consequence cannot be doubted. On the adversaries’ view, with sufficient grace to believe and repent administered to Judas and Peter alike, free will’s good use embracing that common offer put Peter among believers and elect, and free will’s bad use thrusting it back shut Judas out. That stands diametrically against Paul’s word (1 Cor. iv. 7): Who makes you to differ? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why boast as though you did not?
source_text: De consequentia dubitari non potest, quia ex sententia adversariorum, administrata tam Judae quam Petro gratia sufficiente ad credendum et resipiscendum, bonus usus liberi arbitrii amplectentis hanc gratiam sufficientem utrique communiter oblatam posuit Petrum in numero credentium et electorum, et malus usus liberi arbitrii repellentis eandem arcuit Judam a numero credentium et electorum. Sed hoc e diametro adversatur sententiae illi Paulinae 1 Cor. iv. 7, Quis te discernit? quid habes quod non acceperis? quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris ut qui non acceperis?
